comment: Brian (ElevenLabs) VO for Episode 22 (300s): Iraq vs Norway, Group I, real kickoff Wed 17 Jun 2026 01:00. VERIFIED real facts (cited in README): on 29 July 2007 in Jakarta, Iraq won the AFC Asian Cup for the first time, beating Saudi Arabia 1-0 in the final; captain Younis Mahmoud headed the winner around the 72nd-73rd minute from Hawar Mulla Mohammed's corner; coach was Brazilian Jorvan Vieira; the squad united Sunni, Shia and Kurdish players while the country was at war; bombings struck crowds celebrating in Baghdad (reports of ~50 killed). Norway are back at a World Cup for the first time since France 1998 (a 28-year absence), powered by Erling Haaland (Norway's all-time top scorer, 16 goals in 2026 qualifying) and captain Martin Odegaard; Stale Solbakken's side won all eight qualifiers including beating Italy home and away. Group I = France, Senegal, Iraq, Norway. Did-you-know flourish: Iraq midfielder Zidane Iqbal (ex-Man Utd) is named after Zinedine Zidane. RULES: recap Ep21 as OUR PREDICTION (we predicted France beat Senegal 2-1). This ending (Iraq 1-1 Norway) is OUR PREDICTION. Soccer only - round-neck shirts, a pitch with goals, NO helmets/pads. Lines short - never tempo-stretch. Handle the 2007 story respectfully.

lines.text: In two thousand and seven, a country torn apart by war sent eleven men to play football — and for one afternoon, they made an entire nation forget the fighting.
Tonight, that same shirt walks out again. And somewhere in the crowd, an old man is holding a faded photograph.
Last time, we predicted France would beat Senegal two-one. Tonight: the survivors of war... against the sons of the north.
Welcome back to WorldCup twenty-six Legends, episode twenty-two. Iraq versus Norway. The Lions of Mesopotamia... against the Vikings.
And stay with me — because the story of this Iraqi shirt is the most powerful in all of football. It's true, and it's coming.
First, the history. Jakarta. The twenty-ninth of July, two thousand and seven.
Back home, Iraq was at war. Bombs. Checkpoints. A nation split between Sunni, Shia and Kurd.
But the team was all three — Sunni, Shia and Kurd, in one dressing room, playing for one flag.
Their coach, Jorvan Vieira, a Brazilian, had been with them only two months. Nobody gave them a chance.
Then the final. Saudi Arabia. The seventy-second minute. A corner swings in.
Captain Younis Mahmoud rises above everyone — and heads it home. One-nil. Iraq are champions of Asia.
A war-torn nation, the best team on the continent. The greatest day Iraqi football has ever known.
And yet that joy carried a wound — bombs struck the crowds who poured into the streets to celebrate. They danced anyway. They had to.
That is what this shirt carries. Tonight, the grandsons of those players try again.
Iraq. The Lions of Mesopotamia — built on heart, on history, on a refusal to be written off.
In midfield, Zidane Iqbal — yes, named after Zinedine Zidane — once at Manchester United, now the brain of Iraq.
Up front, Aymen Hussein and Ali Al-Hamadi — strikers who fight for every ball like the shirt demands.
With Amir Al-Ammari driving from deep and Rebin Sulaka holding the wall. Underdogs — and proud of it.
But across the line stands a wave of red and a force of nature.
Norway. Back at a World Cup for the first time since nineteen ninety-eight — twenty-eight years away from the biggest stage.
Erling Haaland. Their all-time top scorer at twenty-five. Sixteen goals in qualifying alone. A machine built to score.
Beside him, the captain Martin Odegaard — all silk and vision, the one who sets the machine running.
With Sorloth, Nusa and Berge, this is a golden generation — and they beat Italy, home and away, to get here.
So here is the duel. Iraqi heart against Norwegian power. The survivors... against the storm.
Our prediction — built on a nation that knows how to fight, and a striker who simply does not stop. Watch.
Norway strike first. Odegaard threads it through, and Haaland does what Haaland does. One-nil, Norway.
But you do not tell the Lions of Mesopotamia that it's over. They have survived far worse than a one-goal deficit.
Iqbal slides it through, Hussein gets there first — and the lions roar back. One-all.
One apiece at the whistle, in our story. The storm could not break the heart. Do you agree? Comment LIONS for Iraq, VIKINGS for Norway.
And the old man with the photograph? Legend number twenty-two: the Standard-Bearer. He was in Baghdad in two thousand and seven.

He carries the flag those players raised — the one bombs could not lower. Collect him inside the game. At WorldCup twenty-six dot world, pick three of the forty-eight nations — every goal they score scores for you.
Free to play. Climb the leaderboard, just for fun. No prizes. Hit like, and subscribe: the legends are only beginning.
